title: Al Wynn: Louis Armstrong's short-lived band at Warwick Hall
summary: The tape switches to Al Wynn, who describes Louis forming a seven-piece band to lease dance halls, which failed.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: Try one more. I don't have good equipment here for a camera, it doesn't synchronize, I have to open up the bulb, and then flash it. Let's see, it's simple. I guess I can turn this thing off. Whoops, speaker's on. This is, I'll make a note here. See if this is going up. This is continuing the Al Wynn interview. Okay, we're ready to go. You can talk, I asked about either Louis Armstrong or Jimmy Noon, some of the other bands. Yeah.

Well, I just returned from St. Louis working a season on the boat with Charlie Crep. And things were pretty bad musically in Chicago at that time. And Louis was here, and he was just beginning to reach his popularity. He was just beginning to get into it. So he got an idea to get a band, form a band, and lease several dance halls, and this alternate weekly. Yes.

So he leased the hall on 47, the old Warwick Hall. Oh yeah, I remember. And he got another hall on the west side. I don't remember, it was on Madison Street somewhere, I don't remember just the name of it. So he got a band together. I was in the band, Zooty, and Earl, Joe Walker, Lil' Joe Walker, Frank Sacks, and another boy, George Terence, was on Sacks. Was Lil in the band? No, Lil wasn't in the band, no. He was still married to Lil, but Lil wasn't in his band. Earl was there. Oh, that's right. That's right, true. I don't remember if we had a guitar or not. It possibly could have been packed by, I doubt it, I think we had a tuba. We had seven pieces, I know. I think it possibly could have been Peter Briggs. So that was his idea. I mean we were going to make our own work, you know, and be independent and one of those things. But it didn't turn out quite that way. I mean we worked, we would have a few people out. Because Lil wasn't really too popular, he was on his way up, you know, just another name. So we would play these halls, if he had at least. And the way he had it figured out, we had about four nights. We had about three nights that he was actually promoting, and several other nights that we could fill in the week in order to make a week. But on his deals, the crowd didn't come out. I mean we tried it all for a period of about a month.
I remember Zutty told me years ago, he said in place of being the hot six, they thought they'd better call it the hungry six.
Yeah, that's just our poor. And they were so nice at the end of the night, there wouldn't be any money to split.
I think you said Lil had the Hawker jewelry to keep things going or something.

Yeah, maybe. Some story. In fact, I think Lil did finally come into the band after I cut out and then Earl cut out and they still tried to carry on. So what happened, the people didn't come out, didn't support it. I remember what really topped off everything. He gave a dance free at Warwick Hall, you know. He said, well I just want to see if we can do it. Let's come on in, it's for free, no animation done. Let's come on in. He didn't expect to make anything. So we couldn't have a crowd for free, you know. They didn't come in for free. They didn't come in for free. You know, free. Everything for free. Let's come on in. So they didn't come in. So that's when he threw up both hands and said, well, it don't look like this is it. And of course he was stuck with the lease and everything. He eventually had to pay it off. So that venture didn't work out at all. So Dave Payton had a job. He was for a band going out here at 63rd in the Persian Hotel. He was a club Baghdad at that time.
